## From Categorical Nosology to Dynamical Systems Theory

Current psychiatric classification systems, such as the DSM, largely rely on categorical models that treat mental disorders as distinct entities. However, this framework often fails to capture the fluid reality of clinical practice [@Joober2019]. The limitations of viewing psychiatric conditions as static "essences" have prompted a shift toward Dynamical Systems Theory (DST), which conceptualizes psychopathology not as a fixed disease entity, but as a specific dynamical state of the brain and body [@Maj2005; @Kendler2015; @Joober2019].

In this view, the vast array of neurobiological and psychosocial variables that define a person's mental state can be mapped onto a high-dimensional state space. Within this space, the mental state evolves along specific trajectories governed by the system's underlying rules of evolution. Rather than exploring the entire state space, these trajectories tend to converge toward stable points known as attractors, while the surrounding regions that pull the system toward a specific attractor are called basins of attraction.

In neuroscience research, this view of a dynamical systems in which network activity evolves toward stable configurations, has offered a principled account of persistent neural activity, working memory, and the computational properties of recurrent neural networks [@dominguez2007;@balaguer-ballester2018]. Analogously, psychiatric symptoms can be conceptualized as specific attractors within this landscape. While a healthy individual maintains the flexibility to transition between various attractors, a mental illness manifests when the system becomes trapped within deep, maladaptive basins that resist the transitions to other basins [@Salvi2021; @schefferEtAl2024a; @ngr2025].

## Neural Architecture as a Potential Energy Landscape

While the concept of state space and attractor landscape provides a plausible metaphor for clinical symptoms, precise physical grounding in the brain's functional organization remains a subject of ongoing investigation. It is increasingly hypothesized that the network structure of brain at variuos levels of organization shapes the geometry of the state space [@gu2018]. Within this framework, the matrix of synaptic weights ($W$) is thought to define a potential energy surface, or "landscape", where the altitudes represent levels of neural activation [@watanabe2014].

For example, recent research on connectome harmonics and the eigenmodes of cortical traveling waves suggests that multi-scale structural connectivity provides a natural set of basis functions for brain dynamics [@atasoy2016; @abdelnour2018; @haggarty2025]. Connectome harmonics—the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian derived from the structural connectivity matrix—form the basis or dimensions of the attractor landscape, thereby constraining how neural systems evolve. Spontaneous and task-evoked activity patterns can be expressed as weighted superpositions of these intrinsic eigenmodes. Consequently, structural connectivity (SC) does not merely support functional connectivity (FC); it defines the low-dimensional manifold within which neural trajectories can unfold [@abdelnour2018].

The synaptic weight matrix (W) shapes the spectrum of the Laplacian, thereby determining which modes are energetically favorable, how easily transitions between modes occur, and how stable particular configurations become [@delange2014]. In this sense, it can be understood that alterations in SC or FC reshape the eigen-spectrum, which in turn deforms the geometry of the attractor landscape. Empirical studies using connectome spectral analysis in depression have shown that pathological states are associated with altered occupancy and energy distribution across harmonics, consistent with a reconfiguration of the underlying state space [@atasoy2017].

As the systems' state evolves according to dynamic rules, it behaves like a ball rolling across this landscape. Stable equilibrium points at the bottom of valleys represent attractors, while unstable peaks and ridges act as repellors that push the system toward neighboring basins. The "dynamic resilience" of any given state, as described by Scheffer et al.[@schefferEtAl2024a], is determined by the basin's depth and the steepness of its slopes. In a resilient healthy system, deep basins allow the brain to absorb significant perturbations and rapidly return to a stable equilibrium.

## Hysteresis and Network Rigidity

Hysteresis refers to the tendency for a system to remain trapped in a maladaptive state even after the initiating stressor has vanished. While healthy basins of attraction may be degraded and shallow, pathological states often develop intense local hyper-connectivity, resulting in deep, rigid basins [@SvozCouche2017]. This "trapping" is rooted in multi-scale deficits that span from synaptic architecture to large-scale network dynamics.

At the synaptic level, depression is closely associated with impaired neuroplasticity and structural erosion, including decreased dendritic spine density, impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), and reduced expression of plasticity-related molecules such as BDNF [@Price2010; @Duman2012; @Kang2012; @Duman2016]. These cellular-level deficits translate into macroscopic abnormalities in large-scale functional networks, particularly within the Default Mode Network (DMN) [@Yan2019; @Tozzi2021].

In healthy individuals, DFC exhibits significant flexibility, allowing the brain to transition seamlessly between a diverse repertoire of attractor states. In contrast, patients with depression exhibit reduced temporal variability and a restricted state repertoire. This network rigidity leads to excessive occupancy in sub-optimal states, most notably the depressive rumination associated with the hyper-segregated DMN [@Kaiser2016; @Demirta2016; @DOstilio2016; @Regonia2021; @Durstewitz2021; @An2024].

## Metastability: A Metric for Dynamical Flexibility

One way to formalize this flexibility more rigorously is through metastability, which is the capacity to fluctuate between multiple functional states [@deco2017]. Neuroscientists quantify this property using the Kuramoto order parameter ($R(t)$), which measures the global level of synchronization across the brain at any given instant. Under complete independence, the phases of neural signals are uniformly distributed ($R \approx 0$), whereas full synchronization implies all phases are equal ($R \approx 1$).

Metastability is defined as the variability of this synchronization over time, calculated as the standard deviation of the Kuramoto order parameter: $$ \text{Metastability} = \sigma [R(t)] $$ High metastability indicates that the global synchronization level is constantly fluctuating, rather than remaining fixed.

This temporal variability is interpreted as a hallmark of a healthy, adaptive system [@torres2024]. A brain with high metastability avoids the extremes of being trapped in a "frozen" state of fixed synchronization or a completely disordered state of incoherence. Instead, it maintains a dynamic balance between integration (synchronization) and segregation (desynchronization). This fluid regime ensures that the system does not settle permanently into a single attractor but retains the flexibility to rapidly reorganize and visit a diverse repertoire of functional configurations.

## Therapeutic Recovery as Landscape Reshaping

DST suggests that recovery requires reshaping the attractor landscape. Because pathological basins can be very deep and rigid (hysteresis), small perturbations often fail to dislodge the system. Intensive treatments, such as ECT, rTMS, and psychedelics, may provide enough energy to reset the system, and then allowing the system to settle into a new set of attractors (see Figure \@ref(fig:health_ECT)).

For example, "RElaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS)", which is one of the models of psychedelic action, integrates the "Entropic Brain" hypothesis with a predictive processing framework [@CarhartHarris2019]. The REBUS model postulates that psychedelics, through their $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$ agonism, induce a dysynchronization of higher-order cortical regions [@siegel2024]. This manifests as a relaxed precision-weighting on high-level prior beliefs, effectively decreasing the "stiffness" of the top-down cognitive constraints.

In a control-theoretic formulation, this acute perturbation was described as a "transient flattening of the control-energy landscape" [@Madsen2021; @Singleton2022]. Mechanistically, psychedelics lower the minimum energy required to transition between recurrent brain states, operationalized as a reduction in the energetic barriers separating diverse attractors. Energy-barrier reduction has been associated with shorter state dwell times and more entropic state sequences, consistent with an increase in attractor malleability and enhanced exploration of the brain's state space. Whether through the broad physiological "reset" of ECT or the desynchronization of psychedelics, the goal of these treatments remains consistent: to provide the system an opportunity to remodel the attractor landscape to healthy states [@Rao2018; @Rolls2020].
